title: What Americans Ate When There Were No Food Laws
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck examine American food safety before federal regulation, focusing on the Gilded Age and early 1900s. They cover adulterated milk (watering, chalk, formaldehyde, and calf brains used as fake cream) and the infant deaths it caused, and Indiana health officer John Newell Hurdy. They discuss Harvey Washington Wiley's Bureau of Chemistry work and the Poison Squad experiments, then Teddy Roosevelt's anger over rotten canned beef from the Spanish-American War. The episode covers Upton Sinclair's The Jungle and the Chicago meatpacking conditions it exposed, the Neill-Reynolds investigation, and the resulting Meat Inspection Act and Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906, with a note on the FDA's later creation. The episode ends with a live-show listener mail about the Seattle event and tour cities.

entities.name: Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906

segments.title: Opening and content warning
segments.summary: Hosts give quick announcements, including a tooth implant that may cause lisping, and a content warning about gross food history. They preview the episode: food was unregulated in America's Second Industrial Revolution era.

segments.title: Lack of food laws and Gilded Age hands-off approach
segments.summary: Chuck explains that no food safety laws existed, citing Deborah Blum's The Poison Squad. The hosts speculate on why regulators stayed hands-off, including naivete and reluctance to interfere with a booming economy.

segments.title: Milk adulteration in Indiana
segments.summary: Pasteurization was not widespread until decades after its 1850s development. Dirty milk killed about 400,000 American babies a year. John Newell Hurdy, Indiana's chief health officer from 1896, found watered-down milk containing pond water, worms, insects, blood, pus, and manure. Farmers used chalk, flour, or plaster of Paris to whiten it, and calf brains as a cream substitute.

segments.title: Formaldehyde in milk and Hurdy's quote
segments.summary: Formaldehyde was widely used to preserve milk before pasteurization, and it killed infants, including those in orphanages that relied on cow's milk. Hurdy made a smarmy remark to a reporter about embalming the baby.

segments.title: Harvey Wiley and early food adulteration tests
segments.summary: Harvey Washington Wiley, a Purdue chemist, was hired to run the USDA's new Bureau of Chemistry. He began testing foods and found most honey and maple syrup was fake, made of corn syrup. He then looked into formaldehyde and borax in food.

segments.title: Congressional resistance and the Poison Squad
segments.summary: Congress resisted food regulation bills, with over a hundred introduced and only eight or nine passed. Wiley ran the Poison Squad experiment in 1902, feeding twelve government clerks chemicals including formaldehyde and borax. The press dubbed him Old Borax.

segments.title: Wiley's national profile
segments.summary: Wiley became a national figure. Chuck notes that Teddy Roosevelt, Upton Sinclair, and Wiley were all driving forces behind food regulation.

segments.title: Teddy Roosevelt and the Spanish-American War canned beef
segments.summary: Roosevelt's rough riders fought in Cuba, where about 4,000 Americans died... (the transcript says about 400 died in combat and about 5,500 from disease). McKinley's commission examined rations. Canned roast beef was rotten and treated with formaldehyde. Roosevelt, then New York governor, testified that the beef was a disgrace. He became vice president, then president after McKinley's assassination.

segments.title: Beef Trust and Upton Sinclair's The Jungle
segments.summary: Roosevelt targeted the Beef Trust, the Big Five meatpackers including Armour, Swift, and Libby. Upton Sinclair's novel The Jungle, about an immigrant worker, drew attention mainly to Chicago's Packingtown and the Union Stockyards. Sinclair went undercover for seven weeks and described assembly-line slaughter at high volume.

segments.title: Gross details of meatpacking and sausage
segments.summary: Sinclair described rotten meat, floor scrapings, tuberculosis-spitting workers, rats, and poisoned bread going into sausage. Potted chicken contained no chicken. Workers lost fingers and limbs, and one fell into a lard vat. Sinclair said he aimed at the public's heart and hit the stomach.

segments.title: The Jungle's publication and the business side of reform
segments.summary: The Jungle was released in January 1906 and sold 25,000 copies immediately, then was translated into seventeen languages. Some businesses that already followed safe practices, including the Heinz Company, supported regulation to level the playing field.

segments.title: Roosevelt, Sinclair, and the muckrakers
segments.summary: Roosevelt received many letters about food safety and contacted Sinclair, but the two did not like each other. Sinclair was accused of taking Beef Trust money, which he denied. Roosevelt coined the term muckraker, drawing from Pilgrim's Progress.

segments.title: Neill-Reynolds investigation and plant conditions
segments.summary: Roosevelt had Commissioner Charles Neill and attorney James Reynolds investigate Packingtown. Packers knew they were coming, and the report confirmed Sinclair's account and found worse conditions. Bathrooms were cordoned-off corners with urine on blood-soaked rotting floors. USDA inspectors had limited authority and carcasses rejected could be reprocessed.

segments.title: Legislation passed: Meat Inspection Act and Pure Food and Drug Act
segments.summary: Roosevelt threatened to release the report to push Congress; the Senate passed a bill and the House resisted until the report was released. The result was the Meat Inspection Act of 1906 and the Pure Food and Drug Act, known as the Wiley Act. The FDA was created in 1930, and the Bureau of Chemistry was moved out of the USDA in 1927. In 1938 the FDA received real enforcement powers.

segments.title: Listener mail about Seattle live show
segments.summary: Hosts announce upcoming live tour cities and read a listener email from Mary Benedict about attending the Seattle show with her fourteen-year-old grandson, and the hosts' response to her note.
